claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved high-temperature plastic strain relative to commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved high-temperature toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten.
Severe lattice distortion governs the improved plastic strain and toughness of WTaTiVZr.
Severe lattice distortion induces wavy dislocation lines.
Wavy dislocation lines limit dislocation mobility.
Limited dislocation mobility promotes more homogeneous plastic deformation and work hardening.
The prepared equimolar WTaTiVZr material is a random solid solution.
Testing at approximately 700–900°C is an appropriate elevated-temperature deformation regime for this refractory alloy comparison.
Matching grain sizes and processing histories isolates the effect of composition-induced lattice distortion.
The random distribution of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces severe lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion displaces edge-dislocation cores from their neutral planes and produces wavy dislocation lines.
Reduced edge-dislocation mobility delays localized failure and enhances work hardening.
Dislocations in pure tungsten follow less complex paths that can cause earlier deformation localization.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher high-temperature strain-hardening rate than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater high-temperature uniform elongation than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater high-temperature toughness than pure tungsten.
Wavy dislocation configurations will be more pronounced in WTaTiVZr than in pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conditions where dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates and the alloy is well homogenized and free of secondary precipitates.
Twinning, dynamic recrystallization, major grain-size differences, or different processing histories can invalidate the proposed comparison.
Minor secondary phases and microstructural evolution during testing may affect the quantitative changes in plastic strain and toughness.
